claim: The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau has an average elevation of ~5 km over an area of 2.5 million km2.
source: The Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (QTP) is the most extensively elevated surface on Earth, with an average elevation of ~5  km over an area of 2.5 million km2 (Ding et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ding et al., 2022.

claim: The uplift of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau exerts profound influences on the environment and determines biogeographic boundaries both within and across continents.
source: The uplift of the plateau exerts profound influences on the environment and determines the biogeographic boundaries both within and across continents (Ficetola et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ficetola et al., 2017.

claim: The unique geological developments of the QTP, especially its high elevation, have influenced various taxonomic groups continuously.
source: The unique geological developments of the QTP, especially its high elevation, are believed to have influenced various taxonomic groups continuously (Favre et al., 2015; Miao et al., 2022; Mi et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Favre et al., 2015; Miao et al., 2022; Mi et al., 2021.

claim: The plateau's uplift brings up Asian monsoons, one of the most vigorous phenomena in the global climate system.
source: However, the plateau's uplift also brings up Asian monsoons, one of the most vigorous phenomena in the global climate system (Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Wu et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: Asian monsoons dominate large areas extending from the Indian subcontinent eastwards to Southeast and East Asia.
source: The Asian monsoons dominate large areas extending from the Indian subcontinent eastwards to Southeast and East Asia (Yang et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2021.

claim: The evolution and variability of Asian monsoons have caused significant variations in the redistribution of water and heat via natural processes such as drought, flood, and heat waves.
source: Their evolution and variability have caused significant variations in the redistribution of water and heat via a series of natural processes, such as drought, flood, and heat waves (Wu et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wu et al., 2022.

claim: Most studies that explored the influence of the QTP conceived the plateau as an orographic barrier.
source: However, owing to the difficulties in studying the complex effects caused by monsoons, most studies that explored the influence of the QTP just conceived the plateau as an orographic barrier (Zhan et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhan et al., 2011; Zhao et al., 2023; Lei et al., 2014.

claim: The role of monsoons in shaping species movement patterns remains poorly understood.
source: The role of monsoons in shaping species movement patterns remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A majority of animals migrate latitudinally between wintering and breeding areas.
source: Amongst them, the migratory direction is one of the most prominent indicators for migration patterns, evidenced by a majority of animals migrating latitudinally between wintering and breeding areas (Gu et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gu et al., 2024.

claim: Wintering sites are usually located in the warmer south (e.g. Tropic) and breeding sites located in the cooler north (e.g. Arctic).
source: This can be explained by not only the fact that wintering sites are usually located in the warmer south (e.g. Tropic) and breeding sites located in the cooler north (e.g. Arctic), but also the earth's magnetic fields that are arguably believed to affect the latitudinal migration of animals (Guerra et al., 2014; Gulson-Castillo et al., 2023; Wynn et al., 2022; Takahashi et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is presented as a fact and supported by citations to Guerra et al., 2014; Gulson-Castillo et al., 2023; Wynn et al., 2022; Takahashi et al., 2022.

claim: Earth's magnetic fields are arguably believed to affect the latitudinal migration of animals.
source: This can be explained by not only the fact that wintering sites are usually located in the warmer south (e.g. Tropic) and breeding sites located in the cooler north (e.g. Arctic), but also the earth's magnetic fields that are arguably believed to affect the latitudinal migration of animals (Guerra et al., 2014; Gulson-Castillo et al., 2023; Wynn et al., 2022; Takahashi et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Guerra et al., 2014; Gulson-Castillo et al., 2023; Wynn et al., 2022; Takahashi et al., 2022.

claim: Migratory direction can be changed from latitudinal to longitudinal when animals face environmental changes.
source: However, the migratory direction can be changed from latitudinal to longitudinal when the animal faces environmental changes (Gu et al., 2021; Dufour et al., 2021; Lehikoinen and Virkkala, 2016; McCaslin and Heath, 2020; Briedis et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gu et al., 2021; Dufour et al., 2021; Lehikoinen and Virkkala, 2016; McCaslin and Heath, 2020; Briedis et al., 2020.

claim: Environmental fluctuations in the QTP are relatively small over the longue durée after the final-stage uplift.
source: Environmental fluctuations in the QTP are relatively small over the longue durée after the final-stage uplift (Li and Fang, 1999), but few studies have evaluated how environmental heterogeneity across the QTP might influence the migratory behaviour of birds (but see migratory pattern descriptions, e.g. Zhao et al., 2024, Pu and Guo, 2023).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Li and Fang, 1999.

claim: Few studies have evaluated how environmental heterogeneity across the QTP might influence the migratory behaviour of birds.
source: Environmental fluctuations in the QTP are relatively small over the longue durée after the final-stage uplift (Li and Fang, 1999), but few studies have evaluated how environmental heterogeneity across the QTP might influence the migratory behaviour of birds (but see migratory pattern descriptions, e.g. Zhao et al., 2024, Pu and Guo, 2023).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of research, with references to Zhao et al., 2024, Pu and Guo, 2023 as exceptions.

claim: The distribution of migratory birds extended in longitude and narrowed in latitude with the uplift of QTP.
source: By contrasting their distributions before and after the uplift, we find the distribution of migratory birds extended in longitude and narrowed in latitude with the uplift of QTP (Figure 1E, G, and I).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from species distribution modeling and shown in Figure 1E, G, and I.

claim: Birds are more likely to migrate along a longitudinal gradient in present environments as a result of the QTP uplift.
source: Birds are more likely to migrate along a longitudinal gradient in present environments as a result of the QTP uplift (see Supplementary file 1 for area under the curve [AUC] values for model performance of each species).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the distribution modeling results, with model performance metrics provided in Supplementary file 1.

claim: Before the uplift, migratory birds had a higher probability of breeding across a vast area at low and middle latitudes on the Eurasia continent, including West Asia, Siberia, QTP regions, and even Africa.
source: Specifically, before the uplift, migratory birds had a higher probability of breeding across a vast area at low and middle latitudes on the Eurasia continent, including West Asia, Siberia, QTP regions, and even Africa, whilst their most likely breeding areas move northeastwards to the extreme north of Russia after the uplift.
evidence: The claim is based on species distribution modeling results comparing pre- and post-uplift scenarios.

claim: The most likely breeding areas of migratory birds move northeastwards to the extreme north of Russia after the uplift.
source: Specifically, before the uplift, migratory birds had a higher probability of breeding across a vast area at low and middle latitudes on the Eurasia continent, including West Asia, Siberia, QTP regions, and even Africa, whilst their most likely breeding areas move northeastwards to the extreme north of Russia after the uplift.
evidence: The claim is based on species distribution modeling results comparing pre- and post-uplift scenarios.

claim: Birds that migrate across the QTP in the modern scenario have a higher probability of wintering in Southwest Asia and North Africa.
source: Birds that migrate across the QTP in the modern scenario have a higher probability of wintering in Southwest Asia and North Africa, whereas they had a higher probability of moving southeast to winter in Southern China and more areas of Africa before the uplift (Figure 1D, F and H).
evidence: The claim is based on species distribution modeling results shown in Figure 1D, F and H.

claim: Before the uplift, birds had a higher probability of moving southeast to winter in Southern China and more areas of Africa.
source: Birds that migrate across the QTP in the modern scenario have a higher probability of wintering in Southwest Asia and North Africa, whereas they had a higher probability of moving southeast to winter in Southern China and more areas of Africa before the uplift (Figure 1D, F and H).
evidence: The claim is based on species distribution modeling results shown in Figure 1D, F and H.

claim: Wind cost, temperature, and precipitation are three major factors that influence the overall migratory directions (both autumn and spring) of birds.
source: Second, our results show that wind cost, temperature, and precipitation are three major factors that influence the overall migratory directions (both autumn and spring) of birds, despite the differences in autumn and spring migration across different geographic areas (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2.

claim: Wind cost plays a larger role during spring migration than that during autumn migration.
source: Wind cost plays a larger role during spring migration than that during autumn migration (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2.

claim: A higher wind cost is associated with spring migration, which suggests a greater opportunity for birds to use the wind to facilitate their flight during spring migration.
source: A higher wind cost is associated with spring migration, which suggests a greater opportunity for birds to use the wind to facilitate their flight during spring migration (Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 2 and 3, with an inference about the biological meaning.

claim: Birds choose to follow a flyway of relatively higher annual precipitation and temperature during both spring and autumn migration.
source: They choose to follow a flyway of relatively higher annual precipitation and temperature during both spring and autumn migration (Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 3 and 4.

claim: No evidence is found for strong impacts of elevation and vegetation on the direction of migration.
source: Apart from those three factors, no evidence is found for strong impacts of elevation and vegetation on the direction of migration (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 6).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 6.

claim: Temperature is the most prominent factor in the areas east of the QTP and in the central QTP during spring migration.
source: Despite the fact that wind cost is the most important factor for the overall spring migration, temperature is the most prominent factor in the areas east of the QTP and in the central QTP (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Low wind cost in the longitudinal direction and higher precipitation are priority choices for bird migration in the regions west of the plateau (West QTP).
source: Once they start to migrate in the regions west of the plateau (West QTP), low wind cost in the longitudinal direction and higher precipitation are priority choices for their migration (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Birds migrate across the central and east QTP with increasing temperatures.
source: When they reach the central and east QTP, birds migrate across those areas with increasing temperatures (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 3).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 3.

claim: Higher temperatures act as a major clue in the areas east and west of the plateau during autumn migration.
source: Compared with spring migration, higher temperatures act as a major clue in the areas east and west of the plateau during autumn migration, whereas the vegetation outweighs other factors when birds migrate in the central plateau (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: Vegetation outweighs other factors when birds migrate in the central plateau during autumn migration.
source: Compared with spring migration, higher temperatures act as a major clue in the areas east and west of the plateau during autumn migration, whereas the vegetation outweighs other factors when birds migrate in the central plateau (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplements 2–4.

claim: Precipitation plays a role in all stages of autumn migration.
source: Besides temperature, precipitation also plays a role in all stages of autumn migration.
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results.

claim: Birds tend to follow a flyway of decreasing annual precipitation in central QTP and West QTP during autumn migration.
source: When birds migrate, they tend to follow a flyway of decreasing annual precipitation in central QTP and West QTP and an increasing one in the East QTP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Birds tend to follow a flyway of increasing annual precipitation in the East QTP during autumn migration.
source: When birds migrate, they tend to follow a flyway of decreasing annual precipitation in central QTP and West QTP and an increasing one in the East QTP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is based on data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The initiation of migration is inherently inflexible in migratory birds.
source: It is commonly claimed that the initiation of migration is inherently inflexible in migratory birds (Schmaljohann and Both, 2017), owing to the weak or insufficient responses by migratory birds to adjusting migration behaviour (e.g. migration timing and route) (Knudsen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schmaljohann and Both, 2017 and Knudsen et al., 2011.

claim: Long-distance migrants may face greater temporal or physiological constraints given the varied phenologies en route.
source: This claim is particularly invoked for long-distance migrants, who may face greater temporal (e.g. migration timing) or physiological constraints given the varied phenologies en route (Knudsen et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Knudsen et al., 2011.

claim: A major change in avian migratory patterns in response to environmental change for long-distance migrants can be adjusting migration direction from the latitudinal to the longitudinal at the scale of their whole annual migration cycle.
source: Our results show that a major change in avian migratory patterns in response to environmental change for long-distance migrants can be adjusting migration direction from the latitudinal to the longitudinal at the scale of their whole annual migration cycle.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the study's analyses.

claim: One of the biggest climatic consequences of the uplift of the QTP is the development of a unique monsoon system that has shaped environments across continents.
source: One of the biggest climatic consequences of the uplift of the QTP is the development of a unique monsoon system that has shaped environments across continents (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: One typical feature of Asian monsoons is seasonal climate change, comprising a dry cold winter phase and a wet warm summer phase.
source: One typical feature of Asian monsoons is seasonal climate change, comprising a dry cold winter phase and a wet warm summer phase (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: Asian monsoons consist of several sub-systems, including the northeast monsoon and the East Asian winter monsoons that dominate the weather and climate in different parts of the plateau across different geographical periods.
source: Asian monsoons also consist of several sub-systems, including the northeast monsoon and the East Asian winter monsoons that dominate the weather and climate in different parts of the plateau across different geographical periods.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of Asian monsoons based on established knowledge.

claim: Wind cost, temperature, and precipitation have more important impacts on avian migration than elevations in different geographic areas.
source: Our results show that wind cost, temperature, and precipitation have more important impacts on avian migration than elevations in different geographic areas (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The monsoon system, rather than the high elevations of the plateau per se, is an important factor during avian migration on the plateau.
source: This suggests that the monsoon system, rather than the high elevations of the plateau per se, is an important factor during avian migration on the plateau (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The East Asian winter monsoons start to reach the area east of the QTP in early September.
source: Specifically, when birds begin their autumn migration in early September, the influence of the Siberian High on migration emerges as the East Asian winter monsoons start to reach the area east of the QTP, and their impacts at this stage are mainly reflected by varied temperatures and relatively less precipitation (Gong and Ho, 2002; Gong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gong and Ho, 2002; Gong et al., 2001.

claim: The impacts of the East Asian winter monsoons at the early autumn migration stage are mainly reflected by varied temperatures and relatively less precipitation.
source: Specifically, when birds begin their autumn migration in early September, the influence of the Siberian High on migration emerges as the East Asian winter monsoons start to reach the area east of the QTP, and their impacts at this stage are mainly reflected by varied temperatures and relatively less precipitation (Gong and Ho, 2002; Gong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Gong and Ho, 2002; Gong et al., 2001.

claim: Higher annual temperatures and increased precipitations mean more food resources for migrants.
source: This can explain why higher temperatures and increased precipitation play a more important role than wind cost in the east and central QTP (Figure 2) since higher annual temperatures and increased precipitations mean more food resources for migrants (Hoover and Schelsky, 2020; Jonzén et al., 2007), whereas wind during this period is less strong than that in winter (Gong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hoover and Schelsky, 2020; Jonzén et al., 2007.

claim: Wind during the early autumn migration period is less strong than that in winter.
source: This can explain why higher temperatures and increased precipitation play a more important role than wind cost in the east and central QTP (Figure 2) since higher annual temperatures and increased precipitations mean more food resources for migrants (Hoover and Schelsky, 2020; Jonzén et al., 2007), whereas wind during this period is less strong than that in winter (Gong et al., 2001).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gong et al., 2001.

claim: The northeast monsoon begins to dominate the climate in the southwest of the QTP from around the end of September.
source: This is, on the one hand, likely because the northeast monsoon begins to dominate the climate in the southwest of the QTP from around the end of September (Dimri et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dimri et al., 2016.

claim: The northeast monsoon brings cold wind to sweep the QTP down towards the vast spans of the Indian Ocean.
source: The northeast monsoon brings cold wind to sweep the QTP down towards the vast spans of the Indian Ocean (Dimri et al., 2016), which could facilitate the westward migration of birds.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dimri et al., 2016.

claim: The northeast monsoon could facilitate the westward migration of birds.
source: The northeast monsoon brings cold wind to sweep the QTP down towards the vast spans of the Indian Ocean (Dimri et al., 2016), which could facilitate the westward migration of birds.
evidence: This is an inference based on the characteristics of the northeast monsoon.

claim: The extended Siberia High and associated atmospheric systems deliver cold and dry air masses to the Mediterranean surface in the northwest of the QTP.
source: On the other hand, in the northwest of the QTP, the extended Siberia High and associated atmospheric systems that deliver cold and dry air masses to the Mediterranean surface can also provide positive wind conditions for migrants (Labban et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Labban et al., 2021.

claim: The extended Siberia High and associated atmospheric systems can provide positive wind conditions for migrants in the northwest of the QTP.
source: On the other hand, in the northwest of the QTP, the extended Siberia High and associated atmospheric systems that deliver cold and dry air masses to the Mediterranean surface can also provide positive wind conditions for migrants (Labban et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Labban et al., 2021.

claim: Temperature is more important than wind cost in spring migration.
source: When migrating towards breeding grounds in spring, birds adopt strategies different from their autumn migration, accompanied by different effects of environment on their migratory directions. Temperature is more important than wind cost in spring migration (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical modeling results shown in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: High temperatures usually mean relatively rich food resources for birds.
source: Given high temperatures usually mean relatively rich food resources for birds (Ferger et al., 2014; McCain, 2009), this suggests that birds that migrate across the QTP may focus on energy accumulation during their spring migration rather than reducing flight costs in an effort to meet the energetic demands.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Ferger et al., 2014; McCain, 2009.

claim: Birds that migrate across the QTP may focus on energy accumulation during their spring migration rather than reducing flight costs in an effort to meet the energetic demands.
source: Given high temperatures usually mean relatively rich food resources for birds (Ferger et al., 2014; McCain, 2009), this suggests that birds that migrate across the QTP may focus on energy accumulation during their spring migration rather than reducing flight costs in an effort to meet the energetic demands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed importance of temperature over wind cost during spring migration.

claim: Birds that migrate across the QTP may adopt a 'capital breeding' strategy where birds rely on endogenous reserved energy gained prior to reproduction.
source: This pattern could be explained by a 'capital breeding' strategy — where birds rely on endogenous reserved energy gained prior to reproduction (Stephens et al., 2009) — rather than an 'income' strategy where birds ingest nutrients mainly collected during the period of reproductive activity (Jönsson and Jonsson, 1997).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Stephens et al., 2009 and Jönsson and Jonsson, 1997.

claim: The interpretation of capital breeding strategy aligns with studies on breeding strategies of migratory birds in Asian flyways.
source: This aligns with studies on breeding strategies of migratory birds in Asian flyways (Lisovski et al., 2024).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lisovski et al., 2024.

claim: eBird data provides occurrence records for species but generally cannot distinguish which breeding population an individual bird came from or exactly where it goes for winter.
source: It is worth noting that eBird provides occurrence records for species, but it generally cannot distinguish which breeding population an individual bird came from or exactly where it goes for winter.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of eBird data.

claim: eBird data was used to infer broad-scale movement patterns at the species level rather than precise one-to-one population linkages.
source: In this study, we used eBird data to infer broad-scale movement patterns (e.g. general directions and stopover regions) at the species level rather than precise one-to-one population linkages.
evidence: This is a statement about how the authors used eBird data in their study.

claim: eBird data may be biased by the imbalanced sampling and variation of observers' skills in identifying species.
source: The eBird data may be biased by the imbalanced sampling and variation of observers' skills in identifying species.
evidence: This is a statement about potential biases in eBird data.

claim: Spatiotemporal subsampling was conducted to address spatiotemporal imbalances in data distribution and the potential overrepresentation of birding hotspots.
source: To address spatiotemporal imbalances in data distribution and the potential overrepresentation of birding hotspots, we conducted spatiotemporal subsampling following the method proposed (Johnston et al., 2021; Fink et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the study, supported by citations to Johnston et al., 2021; Fink et al., 2020.

claim: Historical cumulative species count for each bird observer was calculated as a proxy to measure the expertise of bird observers.
source: To account for the difference in observers' expertise in recognising species, we calculated the historical cumulative species count for each bird observer throughout their historical eBird checklists prior to 2019 as a proxy to measure the expertise of bird observers (Kelling et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the study, supported by a citation to Kelling et al., 2015.

claim: AdaSTEM is a machine learning modelling framework that takes space, time, and sample size into consideration at different scales.
source: AdaSTEM is a machine learning modelling framework that takes space, time, and sample size into consideration at different scales.
evidence: This is a statement about the characteristics of the AdaSTEM method.

claim: AdaSTEM has been frequently used in modelling eBird data.
source: It has been frequently used in modelling eBird data (Fink et al., 2020; Fink et al., 2013; Johnston et al., 2015) and has been proven to be efficient and advanced in multi-scale spatiotemporal data modelling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fink et al., 2020; Fink et al., 2013; Johnston et al., 2015.

claim: AdaSTEM has been proven to be efficient and advanced in multi-scale spatiotemporal data modelling.
source: It has been frequently used in modelling eBird data (Fink et al., 2020; Fink et al., 2013; Johnston et al., 2015) and has been proven to be efficient and advanced in multi-scale spatiotemporal data modelling.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Fink et al., 2020; Fink et al., 2013; Johnston et al., 2015.

claim: Version 1.0.4 of the Community Earth System Model (CESM) coupled model was used to simulate pre-uplift environments.
source: In detail, following Zhang et al., 2019, we used version 1.0.4 of the Community Earth System Model (CESM) coupled model with a dynamic atmosphere (CAM4), land (CLM4), ocean (POP2), and sea-ice (CICE4) components to simulate pre-uplift environments.
evidence: This is a statement about the methods used in the study, supported by a citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: CESM and its previous versions have been widely used in climate modelling.
source: CESM and its previous versions have been widely used in climate modelling, for example, Meehl et al., 2012, and are claimed to be capable of broadly reproducing the features of present-day climate (Gent et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Meehl et al., 2012 and Gent et al., 2011.

claim: CESM is claimed to be capable of broadly reproducing the features of present-day climate.
source: CESM and its previous versions have been widely used in climate modelling, for example, Meehl et al., 2012, and are claimed to be capable of broadly reproducing the features of present-day climate (Gent et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gent et al., 2011.

claim: MaxEnt compares the environmental features at presence points to those of pseudo absences to discriminate the suitable area.
source: MaxEnt compares the environmental features at presence points to those of pseudo absences to discriminate the suitable area (Phillips et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 2006.

claim: MaxEnt builds models using a generative approach and thus has an inherent advantage over a discriminative approach, especially when the amount of training data is small.
source: MaxEnt builds models using a generative approach and thus has an inherent advantage over a discriminative approach, especially when the amount of training data is small (Phillips et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Phillips et al., 2006.

claim: MaxEnt is widely used in the study of biogeography and conservation biology due to its good performance compared to other species distribution modelling techniques.
source: Due to its good performance compared to other species distribution modelling techniques, MaxEnt is widely used in the study of biogeography and conservation biology.
evidence: This is a statement about the use of MaxEnt in the field.

claim: When the AUC value is higher than 0.75, the model was considered to be good.
source: When the AUC value is higher than 0.75, the model was considered to be good (Elith et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Elith et al., 2006; Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: Wind connectivity has been identified as a key factor driving avian flying patterns.
source: We calculated wind connectivity to account for the influence of wind, considering wind connectivity has been identified as a key factor driving avian flying patterns (Kemp et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kemp et al., 2010.

claim: The major effect of the plateau uplift is changing avian migratory directions from the latitudinal to the longitudinal.
source: We find that the major effect of the plateau uplift is changing avian migratory directions from the latitudinal to the longitudinal.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the analyses conducted.

claim: The monsoon system generated by the uplift rather than the high elevation per se shapes changes in avian migratory directions.
source: The monsoon system generated by the uplift rather than the high elevation per se shapes those changes.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on the analyses conducted.
